findings.headline: Compensation payments for service failures rising (£21,581 in 2025/26)
findings.detail: Housing maintenance complaints reached 76 in 2025/26, up from 45 the prior year. Compensation payments totalled £21,581. The council is developing a formal compensation policy to standardise these payments. Recurring themes include delays, cancellations with poor communication, and quality of repairs.
findings.matters: Rising compensation and complaint volumes signal service deterioration and unbudgeted costs; the need for a compensation policy suggests the council recognises liability exposure.
findings.figures: 76 complaints (vs 45); compensation payments £21,581
findings.quote: Compensation payments arising from complaints have increased, totalling £21,581 in the last financial year. The Council is currently developing a compensation policy to standardise payments and ensure a fair and consistent approach where services have not met agreed standards.

findings.headline: Housing capital programme of £31,550 million proposed for 2026/27, including fire remediation
findings.detail: The council proposes housing capital expenditure of £31,550 million for 2026/27. Major commitments include £1.3 million for fire remediation works (with £850,000 rephased from 2025/26), £10.7 million for major repairs, and £3 million for home energy improvements. Fire remediation covers two schemes (Whitecroft in Hythe and Clarks Close in Ringwood) requiring fire safety strategy updates.
findings.matters: A lender needs clarity on how this significant capital commitment is funded and how it affects debt service or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £31,550 million total; £1.3 million fire remediation; £10.7 million major repairs; £3 million home energy
findings.quote: The proposed Housing Public Sector capital expenditure programme for 2026/27 totals £31550 million. Significant works to properties, including mandatory compartmentation and new fire doors, are being carried out following detailed Fire Risk Assessment surveys. Funding of £1.3 million is proposed for 2026/27, including £850,000 rephased from 2025/26. The Major Repairs budget has been set at £10.7 million.

findings.headline: 49% of domestic housing stock remains without asbestos survey coverage
findings.detail: Asbestos survey information exists for only 51% of the council's domestic housing stock. The report cites budget and contractor capacity constraints as limiting factors. The annual asbestos budget is £100,000, of which 60% is allocated to removal, leaving £40,000 for surveys and testing. A targeted improvement programme is promised once capacity increases, but no timeline is provided.
findings.matters: Unsurveyed council housing is a latent compliance and liability risk; the council has identified it but not resourced it adequately.
findings.figures: 51% of domestic stock surveyed; £40,000 annual budget available for surveys; £100,000 total annual asbestos budget
findings.quote: Currently, asbestos survey information is held for approximately 51% of the Council's domestic housing stock. Progress in this area is constrained by available contractor capacity, and the need to gain access to tenants' homes. The current annual domestic asbestos budget is £100,000, of which approximately 60% is allocated to removal works. This leaves around £40,000 available to support additional survey and testing activity.

findings.headline: Repairs service demand rising 9% with insufficient budget identified
findings.detail: The Repairs Service received 23,030 repairs in 2025/26, up 1,933 from the previous year. Complaints rose from 45 to 76. The council explicitly stated to EMT on 28 April that the service faces pressure, and the report notes: Additional resources are now required to support legislative change and rising demand. A wider review of resource requirements is underway but no funding decision is documented.
findings.matters: A council admitting it needs additional resources for a core service, without documented funding, signals either budget pressure or unmet liabilities.
findings.figures: 23,030 repairs (9.16% increase); 76 complaints vs 45 prior year; emergency repairs compliance at 84.22% against 90% target
findings.quote: Additional resources are now required to support legislative change and rising demand, to ensure strong Tenant Satisfaction Measure performance can be maintained and best-practice service delivery continues.

findings.headline: Recycling income shortfalls across glass (£47k), textiles (£35k), and trade waste (£19k)
findings.detail: The refuse and recycling service saw income fall short in three separate waste streams, totalling £101k revenue loss, suggesting structural market pressures on secondary materials rather than operational issues.
findings.matters: Multiple shortfalls across waste streams indicate market-wide pressures on recyclables income that may be structural and persistent, reducing revenue reliability.
findings.figures: Glass £47,000; Textiles £35,000; Trade Waste £19,000; total £101,000
findings.quote: income receipts were lower than budgeted for Glass (£47,000), Textiles (£35,000) and Trade Waste (£19,000) services.

findings.headline: Capital programme rephasing: £1.561 million deferred to future years
findings.detail: Major capital projects have been pushed into future years, including Lymington Health and Leisure Centre roof investment (£350k), local plan grants (£384k), and Homes for Ukraine support (£342k), totalling £1.561m.
findings.matters: Slippage in capital spending signals programme delivery risk and could indicate resource constraints or scope changes affecting planned investment outcomes.
findings.figures: £1.561 million total; £350k leisure centre roof; £384k local plan; £342k Ukraine support
findings.quote: Rephasing to future years, included in the outturn position, totals £1.561 million and includes: • Lymington Health and Leisure Centre Roof investment; £350,000 • Local plan grants; £384,000

findings.headline: Car parking income fell short by £173,000 (3% of budget)
findings.detail: Car parking income underperformed by £173k, representing 3% of the budgeted amount, with both meter income and penalty charges coming in lower than projected.
findings.matters: Declining parking revenue suggests reduced economic activity and indicates an ongoing operational pressure on this revenue stream that may not recover.
findings.figures: £173,000 shortfall; 3% of budget
findings.quote: A shortfall of £173,000 car parking income (3% of budget) was partly mitigated by net expenditure savings in planned maintenance.

findings.headline: Homelessness services recorded £224,000 write-off of historic unrecoverable bad debt
findings.detail: The homelessness portfolio recorded a £175k net overspend, driven primarily by a write-off of £224k of historic bad debt, only partially offset by £76k staff savings and £84k additional government grant.
findings.matters: Large bad debt write-offs indicate collection and enforcement issues in homelessness services and suggest current cash flow pressure, raising questions about whether this is structural.
findings.figures: £224,000 write-off; £175,000 net portfolio overspend
findings.quote: Write-off of historic unrecoverable bad debt totalling £224,000 was partly mitigated by £76,000 staff savings and £84,000 extra government grant.

findings.headline: Council creating £500,000 reserve to fund retention of business-critical staff due to Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The council has adopted a Market Supplement Policy in response to LGR and is establishing a new £500k Staff Retention Reserve, intended to fund retention arrangements for business-critical roles through 2026/27 and 2027/28.
findings.matters: This signals significant organisational uncertainty from LGR and indicates the council is struggling to retain key staff at standard rates, raising governance and service delivery risk.
findings.figures: £500,000 reserve
findings.quote: In light of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) the Council adopted a revised Market Supplement Policy to support the retention of a small number of business-critical roles.

findings.headline: Business rates income fell £833,000 short of budget in 2025/26
findings.detail: Business rates, a major council revenue source, came in £833k below the original budget. This represents a significant variance suggesting either economic headwinds or revaluation impacts affecting the council's business rates yield.
findings.matters: Business rates are a council's largest income source. A significant shortfall indicates underlying economic weakness or rating changes that could persist and reduce financial resilience.
findings.figures: £833,000 shortfall
findings.quote: In addition, business rates income was £833,000 less than the original budget.

findings.headline: MTFP forecasts a budget deficit of £1.499 million for 2027/28
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Plan as of February 2026 projects a deficit of £1.499m for 2027/28. The report acknowledges this despite the current year surplus, stating that 'the ongoing requirement to find efficiencies, savings or additional income remains in order to support the achievement of a balanced budget for 2027/28.'
findings.matters: This indicates a significant structural budget gap ahead that the council has not yet solved. Lenders need confidence in how a £1.5m shortfall will be closed.
findings.figures: £1.499 million
findings.quote: The February 2026 MTFP position confirmed the latest forecast deficit for 2027/28 as £1.499 million.

findings.paper_title: Report - SAMP Strategic Asset Management Plan Progress Report - July 2026 Cabinet Final (3)
findings.headline: Internal audit of £107m asset portfolio and governance framework underway; findings expected in late June but not yet reported to Cabinet
findings.detail: Southern Internal Audit Partnership conducting audit of asset management effectiveness across 366 non-housing assets. Scope covers governance, controls, statutory compliance, building safety, and application of Asset Challenge Framework. Audit findings expected in late June 2026 but not included in this Cabinet report dated 1 July 2026.
findings.matters: Asset management governance is foundational to council financial sustainability; audit findings could identify control gaps or compliance risks across a £107m portfolio, particularly material given imminent restructuring under LGR.
findings.figures: 366 non-housing assets valued at over £107 million; Internal audit review in progress
findings.quote: The review covers the Council's estate of 366 non-housing assets, valued at over £107 million and spanning approximately 770 hectares. The audit scope reflects the critical enabling role of asset management in relation to statutory compliance, building safety, financial sustainability, service delivery, regeneration and environmental objectives.

findings.paper_title: Report - SAMP Strategic Asset Management Plan Progress Report - July 2026 Cabinet Final (3)
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation splits New Forest district between two unitary authorities, creating asset apportionment and transition risk
findings.detail: Government decision to proceed with LGR in Hampshire will divide New Forest between two new councils. The Waterside parishes (Fawley, Hythe and Dibden, Marchwood, Totton and Eling) transfer to a Southampton/Eastleigh unitary authority, while the majority joins a Test Valley/Winchester/East Hampshire authority. The council is establishing a Property and Estates LGR workstream to manage controlled transfer of 366 assets valued at £107m to successor authorities.
findings.matters: Fundamental structural change affecting council viability, service continuity, and asset management post-transfer; creates operational risks during transition and requires evidence-led decision-making on asset apportionment to withstand future scrutiny.
findings.figures: 366 non-housing assets valued at over £107 million spanning approximately 770 hectares; four Waterside parishes affected by boundary change
findings.quote: Because the current district is being divided, there is a clear requirement to understand how assets, services and staff will be apportioned between the two future authorities.

findings.paper_title: Report - SAMP Strategic Asset Management Plan Progress Report - July 2026 Cabinet Final (3)
findings.headline: £2m Public Conveniences capital replacement programme commits to demolition and new build at three priority sites
findings.detail: New Forest has identified three public convenience locations for demolition and replacement with standardised modular units: New Street Lymington, Calshot Beach East, and Betsy Lane Bransgore. A fourth site (Library Road Totton) has been deferred due to uncertainty around the Totton Masterplan. The programme uses condition surveys and usage data to prioritise investment, employing a managed Design and Build procurement route.
findings.matters: Material capital expenditure with defined scope and tight timescale driven by Local Government Reorganisation deadline; procurement strategy and site selection reflect shifting from site-by-site reactive decisions to strategic portfolio management.
findings.figures: £2m allocated capital sum for multi-year project; 23 public convenience blocks assessed; three priority replacement sites
findings.quote: As part of the portfolio-wide review, four Public Convenience blocks were initially identified where refurbishment would not deliver a sustainable or compliant outcome and where demolition and replacement provide the most appropriate solution. These sites have been prioritised based on a combination of poor building condition, functional obsolescence, accessibility constraints and whole-life cost considerations.

findings.headline: This is the final budget before local government reorganization removes the council's financial autonomy
findings.detail: The speech emphasizes this is the 'last budget in which NFDC has total control' before 'the Shadow Authority exerts its legal control over our finances'. Local government reorganization is imminent and will transfer budget decisions to a shadow authority structure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's independent decision-making window is closing; future budgets will be determined by a restructured authority with different governance and accountability.
findings.figures: None—governance timeline only
findings.quote: this is the last budget in which NFDC has total control, it is the last budget we can make a difference for our residents before the Shadow Authority exerts its legal control over our finances.

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer has assessed proposed spending as not materially affecting budget position
findings.detail: The opposition presents the Council's Section 151 Officer view that the proposed alternative budget changes 'are not of material consequence to the section 25 statement'. This provides formal financial officer assessment that the new spending and borrowing sit within acceptable parameters.
findings.matters: The Section 151 Officer's assessment of material consequence to the s.25 statement is the authoritative professional view on whether these proposals represent genuine financial risk.
findings.figures: None quantified for materiality assessment
findings.quote: It is the view of the Council's Section 151 Officer that the changes as proposed are not of material consequence to the section 25 statement as included within the substantive proposed budget report

findings.headline: £770k drawn from Corporate Priorities reserve for policy spending instead of planned asset maintenance
findings.detail: The alternative budget redirects £770k from the Corporate Priorities reserve to fund policy initiatives, with the originally planned Public Conveniences refurbishment deferred and reclassified as capital spending instead. This shows a strategic shift in how reserves are committed.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion patterns and changes in planned use indicate the council's financial flexibility and liquidity position during a period of governance transition.
findings.figures: £770,000 from Corporate Priorities reserve
findings.quote: £770,000 from Corporate Priorities reserve instead of using that for the Public Convenience refurbishment, which is then covered by the capital allocation to Public Conveniences.

findings.headline: £1 million capital borrowing proposed for warm spaces programme
findings.detail: Liberal Democrats propose borrowing £1m for a Warm Spaces Grant Programme to create community spaces as warm hubs. They argue this is modest borrowing against the council's existing £132.9m debt and claim it will not 'realistically affect the overall financial situation'.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's debt capacity needs to see all proposed new borrowing and the council's assessment of its proportionate impact on an already substantial debt base.
findings.figures: £1 million capital expenditure; existing council debt £132.9 million
findings.quote: £1 million capital expenditure for the warm places is a sum worth borrowing for the positive impact on New Forest residents and compared to our existing £132.9 million debt this extra £1million would not realistically effect the overall financial situation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - AMR Programme and GF Capital Programme Report
findings.headline: Council is committing to £2.947m borrowing for vehicles and plant replacement in 2026/27, with multi-year programme totalling £7.4m
findings.detail: The general fund capital programme includes £2.947m of external borrowing for vehicle and plant replacement in 2026/27, with further commitments of £1.012m in 2027/28 and £3.458m in 2028/29. Depreciation charges on the vehicles are recorded in revenue and contribute to repayment through Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP). The council also has a separate £610k investment in waste collection vehicles following waste service implementation.
findings.matters: This represents a specific, quantified borrowing commitment that increases the council's debt service costs over multiple years. A lender would need to assess the adequacy of depreciation/MRP repayment rates and whether the council can absorb these costs alongside other spending pressures.
findings.figures: £2.947m borrowing 2026/27; £1.012m 2027/28; £3.458m 2028/29; total £7.417m capital programme (separate from £610k waste vehicles)
findings.quote: The significant capital outlay required will result in older less efficient vehicles being replaced with the latest more efficient models.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - AMR Programme and GF Capital Programme Report
findings.headline: Marsh Lane Depot electrical infrastructure operating at full capacity with safety and compliance risks
findings.detail: Consultant feasibility work completed in 2025 found that the existing electrical infrastructure at Marsh Lane Depot (the council's main service depot) is operating at full capacity and poses compliance and safety risks. The council plans to invest £500k in 2026/27 to install a new 1500kVA substation. The upgrade is described as critical to provide capacity relief, improve resilience, and ensure statutory compliance while supporting future operational growth.
findings.matters: This is critical infrastructure at a key operational facility. Operating at full capacity with safety risks creates vulnerability to service interruption. Failure could impact the council's ability to deliver waste, environmental and fleet management services.
findings.figures: £500,000 capital investment in 2026/27; existing infrastructure at full capacity
findings.quote: the existing electrical infrastructure is operating at full capacity and poses compliance and safety risks. The upgrade will provide essential capacity relief, improve resilience, and ensure statutory compliance, while supporting future operational growth

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - AMR Programme and GF Capital Programme Report
findings.headline: Public Conveniences assessed as critical condition across four sites, requiring £2m refurbishment programme
findings.detail: Condition surveys undertaken in 2025 revealed significant structural and operational issues across the council's 23 public convenience sites. Four priority locations—Calshot East, Totton Central, Bransgore, and Lymington New Street—are in critical condition and require full refurbishment. The £2m investment is phased over 2026/27 and 2027/28, with works including health and safety compliance, accessibility improvements, and sustainability enhancements.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand why these assets deteriorated to critical condition, what this reveals about the council's asset management capability, and whether similar deterioration is occurring in other parts of the estate.
findings.figures: £1.0m 2026/27, £1.0m 2027/28; 23 sites total; 4 sites in critical condition
findings.quote: Condition surveys undertaken in 2025 revealed a range of significant structural and operational issues across the 23 sites. Four priority locations at Calshot East, Totton Central, Bransgore, and Lymington New Street require full refurbishment due to their critical condition

findings.headline: Debt service costs of £5.7m budgeted for 2026/27 on average portfolio of £150.8m at 3.77%, rising with forecast additional borrowing
findings.detail: The Council's budgeted debt interest for 2026/27 is £5.7m, based on an average debt portfolio of £150.8m at an average interest rate of 3.77%. As the Council takes on additional external borrowing to fund its growing capital programme, debt service costs will rise. Investment income is budgeted at £1.7m, giving a net treasury cost position of approximately £4m annually.
findings.matters: Rising debt service represents a growing, fixed claim on the revenue budget that must be funded from council tax, business rates and government grants. As borrowing increases, this becomes an increasingly significant revenue pressure.
findings.figures: Debt interest budget 2026/27: £5.7m. Average debt portfolio: £150.8m. Average interest rate: 3.77%. Investment income budget: £1.7m.
findings.quote: the budget for debt interest paid in 2026/27 is £5.7m, based on an average debt portfolio of £150.8m at an average interest rate of 3.77%.

findings.headline: New commercial and residential investment schemes suspended due to current interest rates making them unviable
findings.detail: The Council has put on hold new investment in commercial and residential property schemes that it had previously been pursuing. The reason given is that current interest rate levels make the economic case for these schemes marginal or negative. This represents a strategic retreat from income-generating investment activity.
findings.matters: The suspension signals the Council is constrained in its ability to generate new rental income streams at current borrowing costs. For a council facing reserve depletion and growing capital commitments, loss of this diversification opportunity weakens its financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Investment schemes suspended; no new loan book impact in current forecast period.
findings.quote: New commercial and residential investment schemes have currently been put on hold due to the current interest rates making schemes less viable.

findings.headline: Pooled fund investments carrying £0.336m unrealised loss, with mandatory statutory override expiry on 31 March 2028
findings.detail: The Council's pooled fund investments (property and equity) are currently valued at a loss of £0.336m against cost. A statutory override under IFRS 9 exempts local authorities from recognising these losses in the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement, but this exemption expires 31 March 2028 for pre-April 2024 investments. The Council has established a Treasury Management Reserve of £0.300m to mitigate risk, but this is insufficient to cover the full current loss.
findings.matters: The override expiry creates a known future impact on the Council's accounts. If markets do not recover or decline further by 2028, this loss will reduce reported net worth and could consume the Treasury Management Reserve, weakening the Council's reported financial position.
findings.figures: Unrealised loss: £0.336m. Treasury Management Reserve: £0.300m. Statutory override expires 31 March 2028.
findings.quote: At the current time, the Council's pooled fund investments are valued with an unrealised capital loss of £0.336m. To date, the statutory override in place of IFRS 9 for local authorities exempts the Council from taking this unrealised loss to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement (CIES). This override has been extended to 31 March 2028 for investments made before 1 April 2024, at which time the Council will be expected to reflect any gains and losses in the CIES.

findings.headline: Balance sheet resources depleting from £53.8m to £35.6m (34% decline), forcing shift from internal to external borrowing
findings.detail: The Council's usable reserves are forecast to decline significantly over the period, from £53.8m in 2026 to £35.6m by 2029. Meanwhile, internal borrowing (using reserves to avoid external debt) is rising to £121.7m by 2029. The liability benchmark analysis confirms the Council will need to access external borrowing to fund the gap between its CFR and available resources.
findings.matters: A 34% depletion of reserves over three years materially reduces the Council's financial flexibility and cushion for unexpected costs. The transition to external borrowing signals the Council's underlying capital commitments outpace its revenue generation.
findings.figures: Balance sheet resources: £53.8m (2026 estimate) declining to £35.6m (2029). Internal borrowing forecast to reach £121.7m by 2029 vs £65.3m in 2026.
findings.quote: The Council expects a positive liability benchmark across the forecast period, due to a rising CFR in combination with an expectation that balance sheet resources will drop, which generally means an authority is required to take external borrowing to fund the gap between its resources and the CFR.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account capital financing requirement surging 132% to £87.8m by 2028/29, driven by housing energy improvements and development
findings.detail: The HRA CFR is forecast to grow from £37.9m (31 March 2026 estimate) to £52.4m (2027), £69.6m (2028) and £87.8m (2029). This represents the dominant driver of the Council's total CFR growth over the period, outpacing general fund pressures. The increases are attributable to housing maintenance, energy improvements and the development programme.
findings.matters: The HRA is normally a council's strongest revenue stream, but this trajectory shows major capital commitments ahead, which will require either revenue surpluses or additional borrowing to service. It signals a significant shift in the council's capital intensity.
findings.figures: HRA CFR: £37.9m (2026 estimate), £52.4m (2027), £69.6m (2028), £87.8m (2029). Total CFR grows from £178.2m to £214.9m over the same period.
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) CFR is also increasing as the Council looks to deliver the requirements arising from Housing Energy Improvements, Planned Maintenance and the current Housing Development Programme.

findings.headline: Long-term affordability explicitly depends on service savings being delivered and continued government transitional support
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer states that medium-to-long-term affordability of the capital programme is contingent on two conditions: (1) service change savings must be delivered as planned, and (2) government must continue transitional support for the waste strategy rollout and HRA decarbonisation. If either condition is not met, the programme becomes unaffordable.
findings.matters: This is a frank acknowledgement of affordability risk. It signals that the council cannot sustain the capital programme from core revenue without relying on external conditions (government support and internal transformation).
findings.figures: Capital programme over 2026-2029: £142.414m total; HRA decarbonisation is flagged as a major cost driver requiring support
findings.quote: the medium-long term affordability remains reliant on service change savings being delivered, and government transitional support (with regards to the waste strategy roll-out & the large decarbonisation requirements within the HRA).

findings.headline: Commercial property investment strategy paused because interest costs exceed expected returns
findings.detail: The council previously approved strategies for commercial (£50m limit) and residential (£10m limit) property investment for economic sustainability and income generation. New expenditure under these strategies remains paused because the council is now in an external borrowing position, and the cost of that debt exceeds the income yields available on investment properties.
findings.matters: A paused investment strategy signals that the council has revised its risk appetite downward due to financing costs, and that investment-driven income cannot offset borrowing costs.
findings.figures: Commercial investment property valued at £28.3m; approved limits £50m commercial, £10m residential
findings.quote: Expenditure on these approved strategies remains paused due to the interest return that can currently be received on cash balances, and as the Council is now in an external borrowing position, the interest charges are currently too high to satisfy the financial parameters of the business case requirements.

findings.headline: Cash reserves being drawn down to a £10m minimum to fund the capital programme through internal borrowing
findings.detail: The council holds £32.4m of investments as at March 2025, but plans to reduce near-term investments from £23.3m to £10m and hold it there. This £10m is identified as the absolute minimum working balance. The drawn-down cash is used as internal borrowing to fund capital spend before external loans become necessary.
findings.matters: Declining liquidity reduces the council's buffer against revenue shortfalls or unexpected costs and increases reliance on debt markets during adverse conditions.
findings.figures: Table 8: Near-term investments 2025 actual £23.3m, 2026 forecast £10.0m, 2027-2029 budgets £10m-£10.3m
findings.quote: the majority of the Council's cash will be utilised over the period through internal borrowing to fund the needs of the Council's capital programme, until minimum balances reach £10 million

findings.headline: Financing costs rising significantly as a proportion of revenue, particularly in HRA (reaching 20.4% by 2028)
findings.detail: Interest and MRP charges on debt are rising sharply. General Fund financing costs rise from 11.5% to 13.1% of net revenue stream; HRA financing costs rise from 15.2% to 20.4%. With HRA at 20.4%, nearly a fifth of HRA rental income is committed to debt servicing, constraining capacity for maintenance and new build.
findings.matters: Financing costs crowding out service delivery budgets is a key risk indicator for lenders; HRA at 20.4% leaves limited headroom for expense shocks.
findings.quote: The Financing costs of both the General Fund and HRA are set to increase as a result of the required Capital Financing Requirement, reducing cash balances (and assumed interest rates) for investment and costs of external borrowing

findings.headline: Total outstanding debt projected to rise from £141.3m to £197.6m over four years, with capital programme debt nearly trebling
findings.detail: The council's total debt is forecast to grow substantially. More significantly, the debt specifically attributable to the capital programme (not the HRA settlement debt from 2012) is expected to grow from £35.5m to £104.1m between 2026 and 2029. This tripling of capital-related debt over four years is a major structural change.
findings.matters: Rapidly growing debt levels increase refinancing risk and constrain financial capacity, particularly important given the shift to external borrowing in a higher interest rate environment.
findings.figures: Table 6: Total debt 2026 forecast £141.3m, 2029 budget £197.6m; Debt–Capital programme 2026 forecast £35.5m, 2029 budget £104.1m
findings.quote: Projected levels of the Council's total outstanding debt are shown in table 6 below, compared with the capital financing requirement

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to grow by £10.5m in 2026/27 and reach £216.5m by 2029
findings.detail: The CFR (cumulative outstanding debt from capital) is growing significantly over the forecast period. By 2029, it reaches £216.5m, representing a £37.6m increase from the 2025 actual of £167.4m. This growth is driven by capital programme spending and limited asset sales.
findings.matters: A growing CFR signals increasing long-term revenue obligations and limits financial flexibility for a lender assessing affordability.
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase by £10.493 million during 2026/27.

findings.headline: The council is shifting from internal borrowing (drawing down reserves) to sustained external borrowing
findings.detail: Prior to 2023/24, the council funded capital expenditure by using cash reserves ('internal borrowing'). From 2025/26 onwards, it requires external loans each year. This is driven by capital programme needs and depleting cash reserves. The council plans to draw reserves down to a £10m minimum before external borrowing starts.
findings.matters: This represents a material change in the council's financing structure and a shift to permanent debt servicing costs on the revenue budget.
findings.figures: External borrowing in capital financing table: £16.992m (2026/27), rising to £21.334m (2028/29)
findings.quote: external borrowing will continue to be required each year from 2025/26

findings.headline: Three property investment assets reclassified and removed from the investment portfolio
findings.detail: The New Forest Enterprise Centre, Totton, and Queensway New Milton have been reclassified due to changes in accounting treatment and operational use, and no longer form part of the 2026/27 investment portfolio.
findings.matters: Portfolio changes signal shifts in the council's asset base and expected revenue generation from its investment activities.
findings.figures: three properties
findings.quote: The New Forest Enterprise Centre, Totton and Queensway, New Milton assets have been reclassified since last year's update, due to changes in accounting treatment and operational use respectively. Consequently, they do not from part of the 2026/27 portfolio.

findings.headline: Council's cash balances are reducing and borrowing need is increasing
findings.detail: Treasury management investments can exceed £80m at points during the year, but overall cash balances have been declining. The council has responded by increasing borrowing to continue supporting its priorities.
findings.matters: Declining cash reserves and growing reliance on borrowing signals tightening liquidity and increased credit pressure.
findings.figures: exceed £80m
findings.quote: overall, the Council's cash balances have been reducing and the need to borrow in order to continue supporting the Council's priorities has increased

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will require additional resources with total implementation cost estimated at £80m-£132m and the council's share yet to be determined
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes £677k for reorganisation preparedness costs, but the wider change programme carries major uncertainties. The total cost of implementation and transition is estimated between £80m and £132m. Cost-sharing arrangements have not yet been agreed, though the council notes it is 'highly likely' to be required to contribute its fair and proportionate share over the next two years. This cost remains unquantified and could prove material.
findings.matters: LGR represents a significant known unknown—a major change programme with costs that remain unquantified but could be material. This adds uncertainty to medium-term financial planning and introduces the risk of unexpected financial demands.
findings.figures: 2026/27 LGR preparedness budget £677k (funded from £2m reserve and revenue); total implementation and transition cost £80m-£132m
findings.quote: Based on the business cases submitted, the total cost of implementation and transition is estimated at between £80 million and £132 million, subject to final Government decisions.

findings.headline: Options to close the £3.43m deficit are predominantly unquantified and uncertain, relying on undefined commercial strategies and savings
findings.detail: Appendix 3 identifies options to close the budget shortfall, but these are largely uncertain. Commercial property investment income and residential property acquisition funds are shown as unquantified ('?') for future years. General process efficiency and accommodation rationalisation have no identified figures. The council acknowledges that delivery depends on 'appropriate opportunities' and potential impacts from business rates, EPR funding, and LGR costs remain unknown.
findings.matters: The council's path to financial sustainability depends on executing options that have not yet been quantified or committed. This represents execution risk and suggests contingency planning for alternative scenarios is incomplete or not disclosed.
findings.figures: Quantified options identified to close deficit: £0 (2026/27), £300k (2027/28), £600k (2028/29), £900k (2029/30); majority of mitigation shown as '?' or unspecified in appendix 3
findings.quote: The current MTFP deficit to 2029/30 (appendix 2) of £3.430 million will be addressed dependant on; a. taking appropriate opportunities regarding commercial and residential property strategies to bring valuable new sources of additional income into the council

findings.headline: General capital reserves will exhaust over the medium term and the £1.2m Budget Equalisation Reserve buffer will rapidly deplete
findings.detail: The General Fund Capital Programme for 2026/27 totals £14.646m and will 'use the majority of remaining general capital reserve balances with current needs exhausting them over the medium-term'. The Budget Equalisation Reserve of £1.2m is explicitly identified as 'limited' and expected to 'relatively quickly diminish' as funding pressures beyond 2026/27 require its use. This leaves minimal financial cushion.
findings.matters: With capital reserves exhausting and the buffer reserve expected to deplete rapidly, the council has limited capacity to manage unexpected costs, revenue shortfalls, or service interruptions. This significantly reduces financial resilience and flexibility.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance £3.0m, Budget Equalisation Reserve £1.199m, general capital reserves being exhausted over MTFP period
findings.quote: the significant emerging funding pressures beyond 2026/27 may necessitate its deployment and will likely relatively quickly will diminish the £1.2 million balance held.

findings.headline: Medium-term forecast shows cumulative £3.43m budget deficit by 2029/30, with deficits emerging from 2027/28
findings.detail: Despite balancing 2026/27, the MTFP forecasts growing deficits in subsequent years: £1.5m in 2027/28, rising to £3.43m cumulative by 2029/30. These deficits represent unfunded budget requirements under current service levels. The trajectory shows the council cannot sustain its spending beyond 2026/27 without intervention—through service reductions, asset sales, major efficiency gains, or reserves depletion.
findings.matters: The deficit trajectory indicates a structural budget imbalance that is only temporarily masked in 2026/27. Lenders assess councils on sustainability of finances over the medium term; this pattern signals rising financial stress.
findings.quote: The medium-term forecast to 2029/30 identifies a projected budget deficit of £3.430 million.

findings.headline: Business rates reset eliminates £4m+ of accumulated growth that had been supporting the General Fund
findings.detail: New Forest had consistently achieved business rates growth since 2013, accumulating over £4m of retained rates supporting the General Fund. The FFR implementation requires a full Business Rates Reset from April 2026, removing this historic accumulation. Business rates retained surplus drops from £4.132m in 2025/26 to £400k in 2026/27, a loss of approximately £3.7m over the settlement period. This is a one-time loss that cannot be recovered.
findings.matters: The loss of £4m+ of retained growth is a material, permanent loss of revenue. It eliminates what had been a growing revenue source and compounds the FFR funding reduction, narrowing the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Business rates retained surplus £4,132k (2025/26) vs £400k (2026/27 onwards); loss of accumulated retained growth £3.7m over settlement period
findings.quote: the effective loss of the accumulated Business Rate growth over the 3-year settlement period results in a particularly difficult financial challenge for the council.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review reduces government funding allocation by £1.2m over three years, compressing available funding from £12.8m to £9.1m
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review represents a fundamental reform of government funding distribution, favouring urban and metropolitan areas over shire districts. For New Forest, this results in a structural funding reduction. The council would have received approximately £12.8m if previous discrete grants had continued, but under the new settlement the 2028/29 allocation is just £9.1m. This is not a temporary pressure but a permanent change to the authority's resource base.
findings.matters: This is a structural funding loss that cannot be recovered through local action—it represents a permanent reduction in resource base that must be addressed through service cuts, efficiency gains, or reserves depletion over the medium term.
findings.figures: Government funding allocation reduces £1.2m from 2025/26 to 2028/29; Fair Funding Allocation £10.0m (2026/27), £9.6m (2027/28), £9.1m (2028/29) vs comparative historical level c£12.8m
findings.quote: Adding £989,000 and £1.5 million to the 2025/26 Legacy Funding Assessment would have seen the Councils comparative funding level at c£12.8 million, instead the reset total at the end of the 3-year FFR period is just £9.1 million.

findings.headline: Rent convergence policy (still contingent) would materially reduce debt by end-of-period, but is absent from baseline and depends on government decision
findings.detail: The council's advisors modelled two rent convergence scenarios (£1 and £2 per week additional increases) which show debt dropping significantly by end of projections and interest cover improving. However, the baseline assumes no convergence, meaning the current plan does not benefit from any policy upside.
findings.matters: The baseline position is conservative relative to recent government consultation; if rent convergence is permitted, the authority's debt serviceability materially improves, but is not guaranteed and creates asymmetric downside if policy reverses.
findings.figures: Baseline assumes no convergence; £1/week convergence would reduce peak debt; £2/week convergence would reduce it further
findings.quote: Both of the scenarios permit the authority to charge additional rent from 2026/27. This generates additional surpluses for the HRA, which enables it to repay more debt. As a result, debt drops noticeably after the medium term and continues to lower significantly by the end of the projections.

findings.headline: Decarbonisation costs of £24,859 per dwelling are embedded in capital programme through 2030 and represent a regulatory commitment independent of council discretion
findings.detail: The HRA plan includes energy efficiency investment to reach EPC level C by 2030 as a standalone cost layer (£24,859 per dwelling at current prices) on top of major works (£51,316 per dwelling). This is not optional and is subject to cost inflation at RPI.
findings.matters: Decarbonisation costs are rising faster (RPI) than rent income (CPI+1% until 2035/36), creating a structural cost wedge; if decarbonisation requirements tighten (e.g., EPC level B), costs would increase materially.
findings.figures: Decarbonisation allowance: £24,859 per dwelling; major works: £51,316 per dwelling; building costs inflate at RPI
findings.quote: The pink area shows an allowance for improving energy efficiency of existing homes to EPC level C standard by 2030, plus wider decarbonisation works. The allowance for decarbonisation comes to £24,859 per dwelling at current prices over the same period.

findings.headline: Right to Buy applications surged following October 2024 government announcement, creating unpredictable asset losses and revenue volatility
findings.detail: The council sold 25 homes under Right to Buy in 2024/25 and expects 40 in 2025/26 while processing a backlog generated by government's October 2024 announcement of RTB reform. Sales then revert to 10–11 per year from 2026/27. This volatility in asset disposals affects both the housing stock available to generate rent and capital receipts.
findings.matters: Right to Buy losses are sudden and irreversible; a policy-driven surge creates uncontrollable revenue loss that the plan cannot accommodate if it continues beyond forecast, risking the underlying income base for debt servicing.
findings.figures: Actual sales 2024/25: 25; forecast 2025/26: 40; normalized rate 2026/27+: 10–11 per year
findings.quote: we have assumed that the authority sold 25 homes under the right to buy in 2024/25 and sells 40 homes in 2025/26, while it processes an influx of applications that followed publication in October 2024 of the government's plans to reform the Right to Buy and reduce discount levels. From 2026/27 onwards we have allowed for 10 to 11 sales pa.

findings.headline: Borrowing requirement is highly sensitive to inflation, rent policy changes, and interest rate assumptions; any adverse deviation materially increases debt
findings.detail: The model assumes specific interest rates (4.8% in 2024/25, reducing to 3.8% from 2028/29) and inflation profiles tied to Bank of England May 2025 forecasts. The document notes small variations in these assumptions drive large changes in required borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on the headline projections as stable; the council's own advisors flag that cost and rate assumptions are brittle, meaning actual debt could be materially higher if inflation or rates diverge from forecast.
findings.quote: The requirement for borrowing is very sensitive to assumptions relating to cost levels, income from rents and other sources, plus interest rates. Initial sensitivity testing of these assumptions indicates that the authority should continuously seek to minimise costs and maximise income as a way of keeping debt levels down and minimising the associated risks.

findings.headline: HRA debt peaks at £169.977m in 2048/49, creating 22-year exposure to interest rate risk from the end of today
findings.detail: Debt rises gradually to £162.384m by 2033/34, then continues climbing to its peak in 2048/49. The late-period peak concentration means the council faces protracted interest rate exposure, requiring careful treasury management over decades.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know when peak debt arrives and for how long the borrowing commitment extends; a peak this late in the projection compounds interest rate risk.
findings.figures: Peak debt £169.977m in 2048/49; intermediate peak £162.384m in 2033/34
findings.quote: Debt reaches its peak level in 2048/49, which is towards the end of the period covered. This means that the authority would be exposed to potential fluctuations in interest rates over the long term.

findings.headline: HRA cannot self-finance capital programme and must rely on external borrowing throughout the entire 30-year period
findings.detail: The council's capital programme for housing investment, stock maintenance, and decarbonisation cannot be funded from reserves, revenue surpluses, or Right to Buy receipts alone. External borrowing is assumed essential to deliver any capital investment for 30 years.
findings.matters: This reveals a structural dependency: the council cannot reduce borrowing even if it wished to without abandoning its capital programme, creating inflexible long-term commitments to external lenders.
findings.figures: 445 new homes to be developed/acquired between 2024/25 and 2034/35
findings.quote: On these assumptions, the authority is unable to finance its capital programme entirely from its Major Repairs Reserve, revenue surpluses generated by the HRA and projected right to buy receipts. This causes the HRA to rely on borrowing to part-finance its HRA capital programme throughout the thirty year period.

findings.headline: Tenant affordability concerns emerging: Tenant Involvement Group flagged impact of rent increases on vulnerable tenants
findings.detail: The Tenant Involvement Group noted 'concern about the impact of increased rents on those tenants affected by pressures on the cost of living', especially for those whose income is not rising in line with the 4.8% rent increase. Approximately two-thirds of tenants receive benefits. The TIG recommended a review of support available and consideration of a poverty strategy.
findings.matters: Growing tenant affordability concerns could drive increased arrears, bad debt write-offs, or policy pressure to restrict future rent increases, directly affecting HRA cash generation.
findings.figures: Average weekly rent increase of £6.10 (4.8%), average weekly rent £133.36 from April 2026, approximately two-thirds of tenants on benefits
findings.quote: the TIG noted concern about the impact of increased rents on those tenants affected by pressures on the cost of living. This is especially true for those whose income is not increasing in line with the proposed rent increase.

findings.headline: Home energy improvement programme costs escalating dramatically: £15m to 2030, far exceeding annual budgets
findings.detail: The council budgets £3m annually on home energy improvements to reach EPC C by 2030, but the total expenditure to 2030 is 'likely to be £15 million, with a further £115 million required to meet net zero targets by 2050'. The aged rural stock with mixed fuel types (oil, off-gas, off-grid) adds complexity and cost. A SHDF grant of up to £824,000 million is expected to offset some costs.
findings.matters: Energy improvement costs far exceed medium-term budgets and will require sustained borrowing or rent increases beyond current assumptions, creating significant long-term financial exposure.
findings.figures: £3m annual budget 2026/27, £15m estimated to 2030, £115m to net zero 2050, 3,200 homes to reach EPC C by 2030
findings.quote: Funding of £3 million is proposed for 2026/27, but total expenditure up to 2030 is likely to be £15 million, with a further £115 million required to meet net zero carbon by 2050.

findings.headline: Aging housing stock experiencing component obsolescence: boiler parts no longer available since October 2024
findings.detail: The council has limited alternatives for maintaining its aging housing stock. Major gas boiler parts became obsolete in October 2024, leaving 'very few alternative options' beyond replacement. The council is phasing boiler replacements but this is now a significant locked-in cost driver with no flexibility.
findings.matters: Obsolescence of key components removes flexibility in maintaining the aging stock and locks in capital expenditure that cannot be deferred, increasing long-term refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Boiler parts obsolescence October 2024, £1.915m heating replacement gas budget 2026/27
findings.quote: Due to the age of a significant number of gas boilers, where parts are no longer available, there are very few alternative options to consider. Phasing of boiler replacements over a number of years has already taken place, following the obsoletion of major parts in October 2024.

findings.headline: Repair demand surge of 30.3% in 2025 is driving reactive maintenance costs and operational strain
findings.detail: From April to December 2025, the housing service attended 26,063 repairs, a 30.3% increase, with potential to rise further. Of these, 1,185 were emergency repairs requiring 3-hour response across the large New Forest geography, creating 'operational delivery pressures'. The surge is attributed partly to Awaab's Law awareness and tenant education campaigns around damp and mould.
findings.matters: Sustained demand surge could exceed the budgeted reactive maintenance capacity (£5.636m in 2026/27), forcing either service quality decline or unbudgeted cost escalation.
findings.figures: 26,063 repairs April-Dec 2025 (30.3% increase), 1,185 emergency repairs, 97.89% SLA achievement for urgent jobs, £5.636m reactive maintenance budget
findings.quote: From the 01 April – 31 December 2025 the housing landlord service has attended 26,063 repairs which demonstrates a demand increase of 30.3%, with the potential to rise by the end of the financial year 2025-26.

findings.headline: New borrowing of £331,000 required in 2026/27 because maturing loan cannot be repaid in full
findings.detail: Despite increased rental income of £1.851m exceeding increased expenditure of £957k, the council will not have sufficient resources to repay the full £4.1m loan maturity in 2026/27, requiring additional replacement borrowing. External borrowing for 2026/27 is £14.045m, a significant increase from the original £12.865m budgeted for 2025/26.
findings.matters: A borrowing decision required to cover debt maturity indicates the HRA's cash generation is constrained, and refinancing risk exists if interest rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: £4.1 million loan maturity, £3.769 million principal repayment available, £331,000 additional replacement borrowing required, £14.045 million total external borrowing 2026/27
findings.quote: there will not be sufficient resources to enable the maturing loan of £4.1 million to be repaid in full during 2026/27 and therefore additional replacement borrowing of £331,000 will be required.

findings.headline: Medium-term HRA operating deficits of £1.1m (2027/28) and £0.6m (2028/29) forecast before rent convergence income
findings.detail: The council's medium-term financial plan shows the HRA will move into operating deficit in the two years following the balanced 2026/27 budget. These deficits will be closed by reducing loan principal repayment to the externally borrowed commitment level of £4.1m, or by expenditure reductions and efficiency savings still to be identified.
findings.matters: Emerging deficits in the medium term indicate the HRA business model is not sustainable without additional income sources or significant expenditure reductions, which is critical for lenders assessing council credit quality.
findings.figures: £1.1 million deficit 2027/28, £0.6 million deficit 2028/29, £4.1 million minimum loan principal repayment commitment
findings.quote: Based on continuing rent increases of CPI+1% alone, it currently shows an estimated operating deficit of c£1.1 million in 2027/28 and £0.6 million in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Bring site operations escalating to unmanageable levels due to fly-tipping, contamination, and illegal activity
findings.detail: The council operates 19 bring sites and is experiencing a recent escalation in fly-tipping and illegal depositing of waste, combined with high levels of contamination of recycling material. These problems are described as now reaching levels that are 'unmanageable based on the current resource level'. The council is requesting £301,000 supplementary for 2025/26 and £589,000 ongoing from 2026/27 to maintain bring site services.
findings.matters: Escalating environmental crime at council facilities and inability to resource management of those facilities indicates operational control issues and rising unbudgeted costs that the finance director would need to account for in future spending.
findings.figures: 19 bring sites; £301,000 supplementary 2025/26; £589,000 ongoing from 2026/27
findings.quote: There has been a more recent escalation in problems, where we are now seeing levels of both illegal activity and genuine depositing of domestic recycling rise to levels that are unmanageable based on the current resource level

findings.headline: Council requesting £1.5m permanent annual budget plus £967k capital for vehicles to maintain service from 2026/27
findings.detail: The Cabinet is being asked to approve £1.5m additional annual budget from 2026/27 onwards to maintain collection service continuity, bring site services, and retain behind-the-gate food waste collections. Additionally, £967,000 capital budget is needed for 2026/27 to purchase additional vehicles. This is separate from a £301,000 supplementary budget request for 2025/26.
findings.matters: The council is locking in permanent additional expenditure mid-implementation of the service redesign, suggesting the original business case underestimated true running costs. This impacts the council's medium-term financial planning and debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: £1.5m additional annual revenue from 2026/27 onwards; £967,000 capital for 2026/27; £301,000 supplementary for 2025/26
findings.quote: Approval of an additional £1.500m of annual budget to be added to the Council's Medium Term Financial Plan from 2026/27 onwards to maintain collection service continuity, bring site services and retain the collections of food waste containers from behind gates

findings.headline: Food waste participation vastly exceeded expectations, causing resource shortfalls and unplanned additional rounds
findings.detail: Take-up of the food waste service has exceeded expectations significantly and shows no sign of reducing. This higher-than-expected participation, combined with assisted collections and behind-the-gate collection requirements, means Phase 1 rounds have not completed on schedule. The council required 4 additional food waste rounds and 1 additional wheeled bin round beyond original estimates.
findings.matters: Budget overruns driven by demand exceeding forecasts indicate planning or forecasting weaknesses, and the continued upward trajectory suggests permanent rather than temporary cost increases.
findings.figures: 4 additional food waste rounds required; 1 additional wheeled bin round; 52.7 additional FTEs by March 2026 (primarily for food waste collections)
findings.quote: Take up of the food waste service across the New Forest has vastly exceeded expectations, and it is essential that residents continue to have confidence in the service

findings.headline: Waste service budget expanding to 41% of General Fund by 2026/27, up from 24.4% in 2023/24
findings.detail: The waste budget grew from £5.5m in 2023/24 to £8.5m in 2025/26, and is now projected to consume 41% of the Council's 2026/27 General Fund budget. The report requests an additional £1.5m permanent annual budget from 2026/27 onwards to maintain service continuity, representing a sustained concentration of council resources on a single service.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial resilience would be concerned that a single service now commands over two-fifths of the General Fund, leaving limited flexibility for other services or managing unexpected demands.
findings.figures: £5.5m (2023/24); £8.5m (2025/26); 41% of 2026/27 General Fund; £1.5m additional annual funding requested from 2026/27
findings.quote: Whilst work is ongoing on setting the Council's budget for 2026/27, it is anticipated that the annual waste service budget will represent in the region of 41% of the Council's 2026/27 general fund.

news_drafts.headline: Compensation payments for service failures rising (£21,581 in 2025/26)
news_drafts.lead: Rising compensation and complaint volumes signal service deterioration and unbudgeted costs; the need for a compensation policy suggests the council recognises liability exposure.

news_drafts.headline: Housing capital programme of £31,550 million proposed for 2026/27, including fire remediation
news_drafts.lead: A lender needs clarity on how this significant capital commitment is funded and how it affects debt service or reserve drawdown.

news_drafts.headline: 49% of domestic housing stock remains without asbestos survey coverage
news_drafts.lead: Unsurveyed council housing is a latent compliance and liability risk; the council has identified it but not resourced it adequately.
